Finish means to reach the end of something — to take something all the way to its completion, so that nothing more needs to be done.

Think of a race. A runner starts, runs the whole distance, and crosses the finish line. That moment — when everything is done and nothing is left — is what "finish" captures.

1. To complete a task or activity

This is the most common use. You finish something when you have done all of it and no more work remains.

  • "She finished her assignment." (She completed it. Nothing was left to do.)
  • "He finished painting the wall." (The whole wall is painted. He is done.)
  • "I finished reading the novel." (I read the entire book, including the last page.)

The key idea here is totality — you didn't stop halfway; you went all the way to the end.

2. To consume or use something completely

When you finish food, a drink, supplies, or any resource, you use up all of it so that nothing remains.

  • "The children finished the cake." (They ate every piece. Nothing is left.)
  • "We finished the bottle of water." (The bottle is now empty.)
  • "They finished all the paper in the printer." (No paper remains.)

Notice that finishing something here implies emptiness afterwards — the thing is gone.

3. To come to an end (used without an object)

When an event, activity, or period of time reaches its natural end, we say it finishes.

  • "The concert finishes at 10 PM." (That is when it ends.)
  • "School finishes in May." (The school year ends in May.)
  • "The meeting finished early." (It ended sooner than expected.)

In this use, notice that there is no object after "finish." The thing itself simply ends.

4. To ruin someone or something completely

In a stronger, more dramatic sense, finish means to destroy someone's career, reputation, strength, or life — to bring them to a point from which there is no recovery.

  • "That scandal finished his political career." (His career is completely over because of it.)
  • "The injury finished her chances of competing." (She has no hope of competing now.)
  • "The storm finished the old bridge." (The bridge is destroyed, beyond repair.)

This use carries weight — it means something is not just over but permanently and completely destroyed.

5. To apply a final layer or treatment to a surface

In crafts, construction, or design, finish means to apply the final coat or treatment that makes something look complete and polished.

  • "He finished the wooden table with varnish." (He applied a protective final coat.)
  • "She finished the sculpture with a layer of wax." (She applied the last surface treatment.)
  • "The carpenter finished the floor beautifully." (He gave it its final, polished appearance.)

Here, "finish" means to take something from a rough or incomplete state to a final, presentable one.

Finish is always followed by a verb ending in -ing, never by "to + verb."

✅ "I finished writing the letter."
❌ "I finished to write the letter." (Wrong)

✅ "She finished cooking dinner."
❌ "She finished to cook dinner." (Wrong)

This is one of the most common mistakes learners make. Remember: after "finish," always use the -ing form.

Finish combines with small words to create new, specific meanings. These are called phrasal verbs, and they are very common in everyday English.

finish off

This has two distinct meanings:

a) To complete the very last part of something, or use the last of it:

  • "Let's finish off the leftovers tonight." (Use up the remaining food.)
  • "She just needs an hour to finish off the report." (Complete the final remaining part.)

b) To kill something or someone that is already weakened:

  • "The second round finished off the boxer." (He was already hurt; the second round ended him.)
  • "The frost finished off the remaining plants." (The plants were already weak; the frost killed them.)

finish up

This also carries two meanings:

a) To complete the last remaining parts of something:

  • "I'm just finishing up a few emails." (I'm completing the last ones.)
  • "Can you finish up what you're doing? It's time to leave." (Complete it so we can go.)

b) To end up in a particular place or situation (often unexpectedly):

  • "He finished up in hospital after the accident." (He ended up there.)
  • "They started arguing and finished up not speaking to each other." (That's how things ended.)

finish with

a) To no longer need something:

  • "Have you finished with the scissors? I need them." (Are you done using them?)
  • "I've finished with this book. You can borrow it now." (I have no more use for it.)

b) To end a romantic relationship with someone:

  • "She finished with him last week." (She ended the relationship.)

c) To be done dealing with someone, often after giving them a reprimand:

  • "I haven't finished with you yet." (I still have more to say to you — usually said in anger or sternness.)

Finish vs. Stop

These two words are easy to confuse, but they mean different things.

  • Stop means you ceased doing something — but not necessarily because you completed it. You might stop because you are tired, interrupted, or giving up.
  • Finish means you completed something — you went all the way to the end.

Compare:

  • "I stopped reading the book." (I put the book down. I may not have finished it.)
  • "I finished reading the book." (I read the whole thing. I am done.)

Finish vs. End

  • End is more neutral and often applies to things that simply reach their conclusion on their own — events, periods of time, situations.
  • Finish often implies an active effort to complete something, or a stronger sense of totality.

Compare:

  • "The war ended." (It came to a conclusion.)
  • "He finished his work." (He actively completed it.)

Though in many cases they overlap, especially for events: "The show ended" and "The show finished" are both natural.

Imagine a jar being filled with water. Finishing the jar means you have poured water all the way to the brim — the jar is completely full, and there is nothing more to add. Whether it's a task, a meal, a conversation, or a career — finish always points to that moment where the last drop has been poured, and everything that was meant to happen has happened.

• Complete a task: "I finished the project."
  • Use up completely: "We finished the food."
  • Come to an end: "The class finishes at noon."
  • Ruin completely: "The scandal finished him."
  • Apply a final surface treatment: "He finished the wood with oil."
  • Finish off → complete the last part / kill what's already weakened
  • Finish up → wrap up the last parts / end up in a situation
  • Finish with → no longer need something / end a relationship
